los.text: Describe the investigation and treatment of heavy periods.
los.html:
Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)Excessive loss that interferes with physical, social, emotional and/or material quality of life (objective >80 mL; clues: flooding, clots >2.5 cm, changing protection ≤2-hourly, double protection, anaemia).
Causes
  • PALM–COEIN: structural: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma (fibroids), Malignancy/hyperplasia
  • Non-structural: Coagulopathy (von Willebrand), Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, perimenopause, hypothyroidism), Endometrial (primary), Iatrogenic (anticoagulants, IUD), Not classified.
  • Many have no pathology.
Investigations (NICE NG88)
  • History (bleeding pattern, IMB/PCB, pain, pressure symptoms, FHx bleeding disorders, contraception/fertility wishes), examination (abdominal/pelvic, speculum), FBC (all), ferritin if anaemia
  • Coagulation/vWD screen if HMB since menarche or FHx
  • TFTs only if symptoms
  • Hysteroscopy (outpatient) if suspected submucosal fibroids, polyps or endometrial pathology (persistent IMB, risk factors for endometrial cancer)
  • Pelvic USS if large fibroids suspected (palpable uterus), adenomyosis or hysteroscopy declined
  • Endometrial biopsy if risk of hyperplasia/cancer (e.g. ≥45 with persistent IMB, obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, unopposed oestrogen, treatment failure).
Treatment
  • No pathology/fibroids <3 cm/suspected adenomyosis: 1st LNG-IUS (Mirena) (↓ loss ~90%; contraception). If declined/unsuitable: non-hormonal (tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic; during menses), NSAIDs (mefenamic acid: ↓ PGs, also helps pain)) or hormonal (combined hormonal contraception, cyclical oral progestogens (norethisterone 5 mg TDS days 5–26)).
  • Fibroids ≥3 cm: refer; tranexamic acid/NSAIDs, LNG-IUS (if cavity not distorted), GnRH analogues (pre-op, shrink fibroids; relugolix combination therapy), uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy (fertility-sparing), hysterectomy.
  • Surgical: endometrial ablation (completed family), hysterectomy (definitive).
  • Iron replacement for anaemia.

los.text: Describe the investigations and treatment of specific causes of infertility.
los.html:
Subfertility
  • Failure to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse (~1 in 7 couples).
  • Investigate earlier if woman ≥36, or known cause (amenorrhoea, previous PID/surgery, undescended testes, chemotherapy).
CausesMale factor (~30%), ovulatory disorders (~25%: PCOS commonest), tubal damage (~20%), uterine/peritoneal (endometriosis ~10%), unexplained (~25%); often combined.
Initial investigations (NICE CG156)
  • Both: history, lifestyle (BMI, smoking, alcohol, drugs), STI screen (chlamydia).
  • Male: semen analysis (repeat after 3 months if abnormal); hormones (FSH, LH, testosterone) if abnormal; karyotype/CF/Y-microdeletions if azoospermic.
  • Female: mid-luteal progesterone (day 21 of 28-day cycle; >30 nmol/L = ovulation), FSH/LH (early follicular), prolactin and TFTs if indicated, ovarian reserve (AMH, antral follicle count), rubella immunity, cervical screening up to date; tubal patency: hysterosalpingography (HSG) or HyCoSy if no comorbidities; laparoscopy and dye if history of PID, endometriosis, pelvic surgery.
Treatment of specific causes
  • Ovulatory (PCOS): weight loss (BMI <30), letrozole (aromatase inhibitor, first line in PCOS) or clomifene (SERM; monitor follicles: multiple pregnancy, OHSS) ± metformin, gonadotropins, laparoscopic ovarian drilling, IVF. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins. Hyperprolactinaemia: dopamine agonists (cabergoline).
  • Tubal: tubal surgery (selected) or IVF; hydrosalpinx → salpingectomy before IVF.
  • Endometriosis: surgical ablation/excision ± IVF.
  • Uterine: hysteroscopic removal of polyps/submucosal fibroids/septum/adhesions (Asherman's).
  • Male factor: lifestyle, treat cause (varicocele (limited evidence), hypogonadism (not testosterone)), ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection), surgical sperm retrieval, donor insemination.
  • Unexplained: try for 2 years total → IVF (NICE: women <40: 3 full cycles; 40–42: 1 cycle; Wales eligibility criteria may differ).
GeneralFolic acid 400 μg, stop smoking, alcohol limits, healthy weight, regular intercourse every 2–3 days (no need for ovulation timing).

los.text: Describe the investigation and treatment of early pregnancy complications.
los.html:
Early pregnancy problemsBleeding ± pain in first trimester; ~20–25% of recognised pregnancies miscarry.
Assessment
  • ABC (haemodynamic stability)
  • Pregnancy test (any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain/bleeding)
  • Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUSS) at Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit
  • Serum β-hCG (serial 48 h) if pregnancy of unknown location
  • FBC, group and save (Rh status)
  • Speculum exam (os open/closed, products in os → remove (cervical shock)).
Miscarriage
  • Threatened (bleeding, closed os, viable pregnancy): reassure; vaginal progesterone if previous miscarriage (NICE 2023).
  • Inevitable/incomplete (open os, products present), complete (empty uterus), missed/delayed (non-viable, no symptoms; CRL ≥7 mm without heartbeat or mean sac diameter ≥25 mm without embryo).
  • Management: expectant (7–14 days first line), medical (mifepristone 200 mg + misoprostol 800 μg 48 h later for missed; misoprostol alone for incomplete), surgical (manual vacuum aspiration under local, or surgical management under GA (ERPC/SMM): if haemorrhage, infection, patient preference, failure).
  • Anti-D for Rh-negative women having surgical management (or ectopic surgery); not routinely for medical/expectant <12 weeks.
  • Recurrent miscarriage (≥3): investigate (antiphospholipid antibodies → aspirin + LMWH, karyotyping, uterine anatomy).
Ectopic pregnancy(~1 in 90; mostly ampullary tube)
  • Risk: previous ectopic, PID/chlamydia, tubal surgery, IVF, IUD/IUS in situ, smoking.
  • Presentation 6–8 weeks: unilateral pain, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness/collapse (rupture)
  • Cervical excitation, adnexal tenderness.
  • TVUSS (adnexal mass, free fluid, empty uterus) + β-hCG.
  • Management (NICE NG126): surgical (laparoscopic salpingectomy; salpingotomy if contralateral tube damaged) if ruptured/severe pain, hCG ≥5000 IU/L, fetal heartbeat, mass ≥35 mm; medical (methotrexate IM) if hCG <1500 (or <5000 with counselling), no significant pain, unruptured mass <35 mm, no heartbeat, able to follow up; expectant if hCG <1000 and falling, stable. Emergency: resuscitate, theatre.
Molar pregnancyVery high hCG, hyperemesis, "snowstorm" → surgical evacuation, hCG follow-up.
Hyperemesis gravidarumAntiemetics (cyclizine, prochlorperazine, ondansetron (after 1st trimester counselling), metoclopramide), IV fluids + thiamine, VTE prophylaxis.
SupportPsychological impact (grief, PTSD), Miscarriage Association.

los.text: Describe the investigation and treatment of fibroids and ovarian cysts and link to disease process.
los.html:
Fibroids (leiomyomas)

  • Benign smooth muscle tumours of myometrium, oestrogen- and progesterone-dependent (grow in pregnancy, regress after menopause)
  • ~1 in 3 women
  • More common in Black women, nulliparity, obesity, FHx.
  • Types: submucosal (HMB, subfertility, miscarriage), intramural, subserosal, pedunculated.
PresentationOften asymptomatic; HMB, pressure symptoms (urinary frequency, constipation), pain (red degeneration in pregnancy, torsion of pedunculated), subfertility, enlarged irregular uterus.
IxPelvic USS (TV + TA), hysteroscopy (submucosal), MRI (pre-UAE/surgery, to distinguish adenomyosis or leiomyosarcoma), FBC.
Treatment
  • Symptomatic: tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, LNG-IUS (if cavity not distorted), COCP
  • GnRH agonists (shrink ~30–50% pre-surgery; menopausal side effects/bone loss: max 6 months) or relugolix combination therapy
  • Ulipristal (restricted: liver injury)
  • Uterine artery embolisation, hysteroscopic resection (submucosal), myomectomy (preserves fertility), hysterectomy.
  • Leiomyosarcoma rare (rapid growth postmenopausal).

Ovarian cysts

  • Functional (follicular, corpus luteum: premenopausal, usually resolve)
  • Benign neoplasms (mature cystic teratoma (dermoid): young women, fat/teeth/hair, torsion risk; serous/mucinous cystadenomas; fibroma (Meigs' syndrome))
  • Endometrioma ("chocolate cyst")
  • Malignant (epithelial ovarian cancer: older, ↑ CA-125).
PresentationIncidental, pain, bloating, pressure; acute: torsion (sudden severe unilateral pain, vomiting → urgent laparoscopy), rupture, haemorrhage.
Ix
  • TVUSS (simple vs complex features), β-hCG, CA-125 (postmenopausal; premenopausal if complex) → Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = U × M × CA-125) or IOTA rules
  • AFP, β-hCG, LDH if <40 with complex mass (germ cell tumours).
Management
  • Premenopausal simple cyst <5 cm → resolve (no follow-up)
  • 5–7 cm → annual USS
  • Larger/persistent/complex → laparoscopic cystectomy
  • Postmenopausal: simple <5 cm with normal CA-125 → repeat USS 4–6 months
  • High RMI (>200/250) → gynae-oncology MDT.

los.text: Describe key elements of a sexual history. Describe presentation, investigation and treatment of STIs. Apply knowledge of STIs to case presentations.
los.html:
• Sexual history: see ICM Year 2 › Reproductive & sexual health › LO 1 (LSI, partners, gender, type of sex, condoms, symptoms in partners, previous STIs, contraception/LMP, HIV/hepatitis risk, PrEP, safeguarding).
STIPresentationInvestigationTreatment (BASHH)
Chlamydia trachomatis (commonest bacterial)Often asymptomatic; discharge, dysuria, IMB/PCB, pelvic pain; urethritis, epididymitis; LGV (MSM: proctitis)NAAT: vulvovaginal swab (women), first-void urine (men), rectal/pharyngeal swabsDoxycycline 100 mg BD 7 days (pregnancy: azithromycin/amoxicillin/erythromycin); partner notification, test of cure in pregnancy/rectal
Neisseria gonorrhoeaePurulent discharge, dysuria; often asymptomatic in women/pharynx/rectum; disseminated (arthritis, rash)NAAT + culture before treatment (sensitivities: resistance)Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose; test of cure
Syphilis (Treponema pallidum)Primary: painless chancre; secondary: rash (palms/soles), condylomata lata, lymphadenopathy; latent; tertiary: gummas, neurosyphilis, aortitisSerology (treponemal EIA, TPPA, RPR for activity), dark-ground microscopy/PCR of ulcerBenzathine penicillin G IM (2.4 MU single dose early); Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction
Trichomonas vaginalisFrothy yellow-green offensive discharge, vulvitis, "strawberry cervix"NAAT, wet mountMetronidazole 500 mg BD 7 days
Genital herpes (HSV-1/2)Painful vesicles/ulcers, dysuria, systemic symptoms (primary)PCR swab of lesionAciclovir 400 mg TDS 5 days; suppressive if recurrent
Anogenital warts (HPV 6, 11)Painless papulesClinicalPodophyllotoxin, imiquimod, cryotherapy; HPV vaccine
HIV, hepatitis B/CSerologySee 205
Mycoplasma genitaliumUrethritis, PIDNAAT (resistance testing)Doxycycline then azithromycin/moxifloxacin
Not STIs but commonBacterial vaginosis (fishy discharge, clue cells: metronidazole), candida (itchy white discharge: clotrimazole/fluconazole).
Case approach
  • Symptoms + exam + sexual history
  • → appropriate swabs
  • → treat (often empirically for syndromes)
  • → partner notification, abstain until treated, full STI screen (HIV, syphilis), contraception, safeguarding, health promotion (condoms, vaccines, PrEP).

los.text: Discuss ethical dilemmas in IVF / donor insemination.
sessions: MHS: Ethical considerations with reproductive treatments
los.html:
IVF/donor insemination ethical dilemmas
  • Access and justice: NHS funding criteria (age, BMI, smoking, previous children, same-sex couples, single women), "postcode lottery", number of cycles; private sector costs → inequity.
  • Embryo status: creation of surplus embryos, freezing, disposal, research (14-day rule), moral status (gradualist vs conception view).
  • Embryo selection: PGT-M for serious genetic disease (HFEA-licensed list), PGT-A (aneuploidy screening: uncertain benefit), sex selection (banned for non-medical reasons in UK), "saviour siblings" (HLA matching: permitted case by case), disability rights critique.
  • Donor gametes: donor anonymity (UK donors identifiable to offspring at 18 since 2005) vs privacy; payment/compensation (£986 per egg donation cycle); limits on number of families per donor (10); disclosure to children; consanguinity risk; international gamete trade.
  • Welfare of the child (HFE Act: consider need for supportive parenting).
  • Surrogacy (legal in UK, non-commercial; parental orders), posthumous conception (consent), older mothers, egg freezing for social reasons, multiple pregnancy risks (single embryo transfer policy).
  • Mitochondrial donation ("three-parent babies": legal in UK since 2015).
  • Consent, counselling, religious views, commodification of reproduction, research on embryos.
RegulationHuman Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990/2008; HFEA licenses clinics, research, PGT conditions, data.
PrinciplesAutonomy (reproductive liberty), beneficence (welfare of child), non-maleficence (OHSS, multiple births), justice (access).

los.text: Identify the musculoskeletal structures of the pelvis and perineum and link them to function.
los.html:
Female pelvic floor and perineum (continence anatomy)
  • Pelvic diaphragm: levator ani (pubococcygeus incl. puborectalis, pubovaginalis; iliococcygeus) + coccygeus; supports pelvic organs, maintains continence (puborectalis sling, compression of urethra/vagina/rectum), resists ↑ intra-abdominal pressure. Nerve to levator ani (S3–4), pudendal.
  • Perineal membrane and deep perineal pouch: external urethral sphincter (striated, voluntary; pudendal nerve), compressor urethrae, urethrovaginal sphincter.
  • Perineal body: central fibromuscular node (attachments of levator ani, bulbospongiosus, transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter) → key to pelvic floor integrity (obstetric tears).
  • Endopelvic fascia/ligaments: pubourethral ligaments and anterior vaginal wall support ("hammock" hypothesis: urethra compressed against supportive layer during coughing), uterosacral and cardinal ligaments (uterine/vault support), arcus tendineus.
Link to function
  • Stress urinary incontinence: leakage on cough/sneeze/exercise due to urethral hypermobility (weak pelvic floor/fascial support after childbirth, ageing, menopause, obesity, chronic cough) and/or intrinsic sphincter deficiency → pelvic floor muscle training (≥3 months, first line), weight loss, duloxetine, surgery (colposuspension, autologous fascial sling, bulking agents; mesh tapes paused/restricted in UK).
  • Urge incontinence/overactive bladder: detrusor overactivity (not structural) → bladder training, antimuscarinics (oxybutynin: avoid in frail elderly), mirabegron (β3 agonist), botox.
  • Pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, rectocele, uterine/vault prolapse) from weakened supports.

los.text: Describe the role of screening programmes and to understand the evidence base for specific current screening programmes.
los.html:
Screening
  • Systematically testing an asymptomatic population to identify individuals at higher risk of a condition who may benefit from further tests/treatment.
  • UK National Screening Committee advises
  • Programmes run by Public Health Wales (Screening Division).
Wilson & Jungner criteria (1968)
  • Important health problem
  • Natural history understood with a latent/early detectable stage
  • Suitable, acceptable test
  • Effective treatment, better early
  • Facilities available
  • Agreed policy on whom to treat
  • Cost-effective
  • Continuous process.
Test performanceSensitivity, specificity, PPV (depends on prevalence), NPV.
Biases
  • Lead-time bias (earlier diagnosis appears to prolong survival)
  • Length-time bias (detects slow-growing disease)
  • Overdiagnosis (detects disease that would never cause harm)
  • Selection bias (healthy volunteers).
  • Antenatal screening programmes (Antenatal Screening Wales) and evidence:
  • Infectious diseases: HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis (treatment prevents vertical transmission: high effectiveness).
  • Sickle cell and thalassaemia (all women; partner testing).
  • Blood group and antibodies (anti-D prophylaxis prevents haemolytic disease of the newborn).
  • Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes: combined test (11–14 weeks: nuchal translucency + PAPP-A + β-hCG + age), quadruple test (15–20 weeks); higher chance (≥1 in 150) → NIPT (cell-free DNA; >99% sensitivity for T21 but a screening test) or diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis (~0.5% miscarriage risk).
  • Fetal anomaly scan (18+0–20+6 weeks: structural anomalies; detection rates vary by condition).
  • Gestational diabetes (risk factor-based OGTT), pre-eclampsia (BP/urine), fetal growth (SFH), newborn screening (blood spot, hearing, NIPE).
Ethics of antenatal screening
  • Informed choice (opt-in, non-directive counselling)
  • Anxiety and false positives
  • Decisions about termination
  • Disability rights critique ("expressivist objection")
  • Right not to know
  • Equity of access
  • Partner involvement
  • Incidental findings.

los.text: Identify the major causes of childhood morbidity and mortality in the UK.
los.html:
UK infant mortality(deaths <1 year per 1,000 live births)~4; higher than many comparable European countries; strong deprivation gradient and higher in Black and Asian babies.
Causes of infant deaths
  • Immaturity/prematurity-related conditions (leading: ~⅓–½ of neonatal deaths)
  • Congenital anomalies (~⅓)
  • Sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI/SIDS)
  • Infections (sepsis, meningitis, pneumonia)
  • Birth asphyxia/hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
  • Injuries.
Childhood (1–18) deathsInjuries/accidents (road traffic, drowning, falls), cancer (leukaemia, brain tumours), chronic conditions (neurological, cardiac), suicide/self-harm (adolescents), infections, asthma.
Childhood morbidityRespiratory (asthma, bronchiolitis), mental health (anxiety, depression, self-harm, eating disorders, ADHD/ASD), obesity, dental caries, neurodisability, allergies/eczema, injuries, diabetes, epilepsy.
Risk factors
  • Maternal smoking
  • Obesity
  • Age (<20, >40)
  • Deprivation
  • Low birthweight/prematurity
  • Consanguinity (some congenital conditions)
  • Multiple pregnancy
  • Unsafe sleep (co-sleeping after alcohol/drugs, prone position, overheating)
  • Lack of breastfeeding
  • Poor housing.
Prevention
  • Smoking cessation in pregnancy
  • Safe sleep advice ("back to sleep" reduced SIDS ~80%)
  • Breastfeeding
  • Vaccination
  • Antenatal care and screening
  • Neonatal care
  • Injury prevention
  • Child Death Review (Wales: Child Death Review Programme).

los.text: Describe the symptoms associated with menopause and how it could affect quality of life and suggest options for management.
los.html:
Menopause
  • Permanent cessation of menstruation for 12 months due to loss of ovarian follicular activity
  • Average age 51 (UK).
  • Perimenopause: irregular cycles and symptoms preceding it.
Symptoms
  • Vasomotor: hot flushes, night sweats (~75%; may last ~7+ years).
  • Psychological/cognitive: low mood, anxiety, irritability, "brain fog", memory/concentration problems, sleep disturbance, fatigue.
  • Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (vaginal atrophy): vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, itching, urinary frequency/urgency, recurrent UTIs.
  • Musculoskeletal: joint and muscle aches; ↓ libido; skin/hair changes; palpitations; altered periods.
  • Long-term: osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease (loss of oestrogen protection), weight gain/central adiposity.
Impact on quality of lifeWork (absence, reduced performance, leaving jobs), relationships, sexual function, mental health, sleep.
DiagnosisClinical in women >45 with typical symptoms (no FSH test needed); FSH only if 40–45 with symptoms, or <40 (POI).
Management options
  • Lifestyle (exercise, weight, smoking, alcohol, caffeine, layered clothing)
  • HRT (most effective for vasomotor symptoms; see LO 13)
  • Vaginal oestrogen (GSM; safe long-term, can be used with HRT)
  • Vaginal moisturisers/lubricants
  • CBT (vasomotor symptoms, mood, sleep)
  • Non-hormonal drugs (SSRIs/SNRIs (not with tamoxifen: paroxetine/fluoxetine CYP2D6), gabapentin, clonidine, fezolinetant (NK3 receptor antagonist: newer))
  • Testosterone for low libido (specialist)
  • Bone protection.

los.text: Describe possible causes for a premature menopause
los.html:
Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI)
  • Loss of ovarian function <40 years (~1%): oligo/amenorrhoea ≥4 months + raised FSH (>25–30 IU/L) on two samples ≥4–6 weeks apart + ↓ oestradiol.
  • (Early menopause: 40–45.)
Causes
  • Idiopathic (majority).
  • Iatrogenic: chemotherapy (alkylating agents), pelvic radiotherapy, bilateral oophorectomy/ovarian surgery (endometriosis), hysterectomy (earlier menopause).
  • Genetic: Turner syndrome (45,X/mosaic), fragile X premutation (FMR1), other X chromosome abnormalities, galactosaemia, family history.
  • Autoimmune: associated with Addison's, thyroid disease, T1DM, coeliac, vitiligo (adrenal/ovarian antibodies).
  • Infection: mumps oophoritis, TB, CMV.
  • Metabolic/toxic: smoking (earlier menopause), galactosaemia.
InvestigationsFSH/LH, oestradiol, karyotype, FMR1 testing, adrenal (21-hydroxylase) and thyroid antibodies, TFTs, prolactin, DEXA.
Management
  • HRT or combined hormonal contraception until at least natural menopause age (~51) (protect bone, cardiovascular, cognitive health; not just symptom relief)
  • Fertility counselling (egg donation/IVF; small chance of spontaneous conception ~5–10%)
  • Psychological support (Daisy Network)
  • Bone health
  • CV risk management.

los.text: Discuss approaches to improve health during and after the menopause
los.html:
• Promoting health during/after menopause (window for prevention):
    • Bone health: weight-bearing and resistance exercise, calcium (~700–1200 mg/day) and vitamin D (10 μg/day), stop smoking, limit alcohol, fracture risk assessment (FRAX/QFracture ± DEXA), HRT (prevents osteoporotic fractures), bisphosphonates if high risk.
    • Cardiovascular health: BP, lipids, glucose screening (NHS Health Check/Wales equivalents), healthy diet (Mediterranean), weight management (central adiposity), physical activity (150 min/week), smoking cessation.
    • Mental health and cognition: CBT, social engagement, sleep hygiene, address mood symptoms.
    • Genitourinary health: vaginal oestrogen/moisturisers, pelvic floor exercises (continence, prolapse prevention).
    • Cancer screening: breast screening (50–70 in Wales: Breast Test Wales every 3 years), cervical screening (to 64), bowel screening (FIT 50–74).
    • Sexual health: contraception until 1 year after LMP if >50 (2 years if <50), STI awareness.
    • Workplace support: menopause policies, reasonable adjustments (Equality Act).
    • Education and shared decision-making about HRT (benefits/risks; NICE NG23 2024 update).

los.text: Describe the indications, contraindications and drugs for menopausal symptoms
los.html:
HRT indications
  • Vasomotor symptoms (first line, most effective)
  • Low mood associated with menopause
  • Genitourinary symptoms (vaginal oestrogen)
  • Premature ovarian insufficiency/early menopause (until ~51)
  • Osteoporosis prevention (in younger postmenopausal women when other options unsuitable)
  • Reduced libido (testosterone add-on).
Contraindications
  • Current/past breast cancer (or other oestrogen-dependent cancer)
  • Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding
  • Untreated endometrial hyperplasia
  • Active/recent VTE (transdermal may be considered with specialist advice)
  • Active arterial thromboembolic disease (MI, stroke)
  • Active liver disease with abnormal LFTs
  • Pregnancy
  • Porphyria
  • Caution: migraine with aura (prefer transdermal), uncontrolled hypertension, high CVD risk, gallbladder disease.
Regimens
  • Uterus present: oestrogen + progestogen (protect endometrium from hyperplasia/cancer): cyclical/sequential (monthly bleed; perimenopausal/LMP <12 months) or continuous combined (no bleeds; postmenopausal >12 months); progestogen options: oral (micronised progesterone (Utrogestan): lower breast cancer/VTE risk), transdermal combined patches, LNG-IUS (also contraception).
  • No uterus (hysterectomy): oestrogen only.
  • Oestrogen routes: transdermal (patch, gel, spray: no ↑ VTE risk, preferred if BMI >30, VTE risk, migraine) or oral (estradiol).
  • Vaginal oestrogen (estriol cream, estradiol tablets/ring) for GSM; tibolone (synthetic steroid); testosterone gel (libido).
Risks (NICE 2024)
  • Breast cancer (small ↑ with combined HRT, related to duration; little/no ↑ with oestrogen-only)
  • VTE (↑ with oral, not transdermal)
  • Stroke (small ↑ with oral)
  • Endometrial cancer (oestrogen-only in women with uterus)
  • Gallbladder disease.
  • Benefits: symptom relief, ↓ osteoporotic fractures, ↓ colorectal cancer, no ↑ CVD if started <60 (may be protective).
Side effectsBreast tenderness, nausea, headache, bloating, irregular bleeding (investigate if persistent >6 months or after amenorrhoea on continuous combined).
Review3 months then annually; no arbitrary time limit.

los.text: Biopsychosocial factors of menopause
los.html:
Biological
  • ↓ oestrogen → vasomotor symptoms, sleep disruption, GSM, bone loss, CV changes, weight redistribution
  • Genetic factors (age at menopause), comorbidities, surgical/iatrogenic menopause (often abrupt, severe symptoms).
Psychological
  • Mood changes
  • Anxiety
  • Depression risk (especially with previous depression/PMDD)
  • Self-esteem and body image
  • Cognitive symptoms
  • Attitudes and expectations (negative beliefs → worse symptom experience)
  • Stress
  • Coping style
  • Meaning of loss of fertility.
Social
FactorExamples
Life stage"Sandwich generation" (caring for children and parents), children leaving home
RelationshipsRelationship and sexual changes
WorkDisclosure, stigma, lack of support, reduced hours or leaving work
SocioeconomicAccess to information and HRT
CultureSymptom reporting varies (hot flushes reported less in some Asian cultures); freedom vs loss of youth
OtherMedia discourse, gender identity (trans/non-binary people)
  • Implications: holistic assessment (symptoms, mood, sleep, relationships, work, health beliefs), shared decision-making, combine medical (HRT), psychological (CBT) and social/workplace support
    • recognise inequities in access.

los.text: Elicit a focused gynaecological history, demonstrating sensitivity and tailoring questions to the clinical context
sessions: Gynaecological history, PV and speculum examination
los.html:
Approach
  • Private setting, sensitive, non-judgemental
  • Explain why questions are asked
  • Offer chaperone
  • Tailor depth to presentation (e.g. bleeding, pain, discharge, subfertility, prolapse).
Structure
  • PC/HPC: e.g. bleeding (pattern, volume, clots, flooding, IMB/PCB, postmenopausal bleeding), pain (cyclical? dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia (superficial/deep), chronic pelvic pain), discharge (colour, odour, itch), urinary/bowel symptoms, prolapse symptoms, systemic symptoms.
  • Menstrual history: LMP, menarche, cycle length/regularity, duration of bleeding, menopause (age, symptoms, HRT).
  • Obstetric history: gravidity/parity, outcomes (deliveries, miscarriages, terminations, ectopics), complications.
  • Contraception: current/past methods, pregnancy possibility.
  • Sexual history: partners, STI risk, dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding.
  • Cervical screening: last smear, results, treatment (LLETZ), HPV vaccination.
  • PMH/PSH (abdominal/pelvic surgery, PID, endometriosis), drug history (anticoagulants, hormonal treatments, tamoxifen), allergies, FH (breast/ovarian/endometrial/bowel cancer: BRCA/Lynch), social (smoking, alcohol, occupation, relationships, safeguarding/domestic abuse).
  • ICE, impact on life.

los.text: Perform a bimanual and speculum examination safely, with appropriate consent and consideration for patient dignity
sessions: Gynaecological history, PV and speculum examination
los.html:
Consent and dignity
  • Explain purpose and procedure
  • Verbal consent (documented)
  • Chaperone (offer, document)
  • Privacy (curtains, cover sheet)
  • Patient empties bladder
  • Warm speculum/lubricant
  • Right to stop at any time
  • Consider trauma history/cultural needs
  • Appropriate speculum size.
PositionSupine, knees bent and apart (or left lateral/Sims' for prolapse).
External inspectionVulva, labia, clitoris, introitus, perineum: lesions, ulcers, warts, discharge, atrophy, FGM, prolapse (ask to cough/bear down).
Speculum (Cusco bivalve)
  • Lubricate (water-based)
  • Insert closed blades obliquely then rotate to horizontal
  • Directed posteriorly/downwards
  • Open gently to visualise cervix (os: closed/open; ectropion, polyps, lesions, discharge, contact bleeding)
  • Vaginal walls
  • Take swabs/cervical sample if needed
  • Close partially and withdraw while rotating, inspecting vaginal walls.
  • Sims' speculum for prolapse assessment.
Bimanual examination
  • Two lubricated fingers of gloved hand in vagina
  • Other hand on abdomen above symphysis: cervix (consistency, cervical motion tenderness/excitation → PID/ectopic)
  • Uterus (size in weeks, position (anteverted/retroverted), mobility, tenderness, regularity: fibroids)
  • Adnexa (masses, tenderness)
  • Pouch of Douglas (nodules: endometriosis, fluid).
AfterRemove gloves, cover patient, allow to dress privately, explain findings, document (incl. chaperone).

los.text: Summarise and present clinical findings clearly, using a structured and professional format appropriate for handover or discussion
sessions: Gynaecological history, PV and speculum examination
los.html:
Structure (SBAR for handover, or clinical presentation)
  • Situation: "Ms X, 32, presenting with 6 weeks of heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure."
  • Background: relevant history (G2P2, LMP, contraception, smear history, PMH, drugs, FH).
  • Assessment: observations; abdominal exam ("non-tender, 16-week-size irregular mass arising from the pelvis"); speculum ("healthy-looking cervix, no discharge or bleeding"); bimanual ("bulky, irregular, non-tender, mobile uterus consistent with ~14 weeks' size; no adnexal masses or cervical excitation"); bedside tests (urine hCG negative, dipstick).
  • Recommendation: "Likely fibroids; plan FBC, pelvic USS, consider tranexamic acid and gynaecology referral."
Tips
  • Be concise
  • Objective
  • Logical (positives then key negatives)
  • Professional terminology (anteverted, bulky, cervical excitation, adnexal)
  • Mention chaperone/consent in documentation
  • Give differential and plan
  • State urgency (e.g. "haemodynamically stable/unstable").

los.text: Apply clinical reasoning to formulate and prioritise a differential diagnosis based on history and examination
sessions: Gynaecological history, PV and speculum examination
los.html:
• Prioritise: dangerous/emergency first (ectopic, torsion, sepsis, haemorrhage), then most likely.
PresentationDifferential (priority)
Acute pelvic pain (reproductive age)Ectopic pregnancy (always β-hCG), ovarian torsion, ruptured/haemorrhagic cyst, PID/tubo-ovarian abscess, miscarriage, appendicitis, UTI/pyelonephritis, renal colic, endometriosis, mittelschmerz
Abnormal uterine bleedingPregnancy-related (miscarriage, ectopic), fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, cervical cancer/ectropion, coagulopathy, hormonal/contraceptive, PCOS, thyroid
Postmenopausal bleedingEndometrial cancer (until excluded: 2WW; TVUSS endometrial thickness ≥4 mm → biopsy/hysteroscopy), atrophic vaginitis, polyps, HRT, cervical cancer
Postcoital bleedingCervical ectropion, cervical cancer, cervicitis (chlamydia), polyps, atrophic vaginitis
Vaginal dischargeBV, candida, trichomonas, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, foreign body, cervical ectropion, malignancy
Chronic pelvic pain/dyspareuniaEndometriosis, adenomyosis, PID sequelae, IBS, interstitial cystitis, adhesions, pelvic congestion, musculoskeletal, psychological factors
Pelvic massFibroids, ovarian cyst/cancer, pregnancy, full bladder
  • Use features: pregnancy status, timing in cycle, fever, cervical excitation, sudden vs gradual onset, haemodynamics, age (menopausal status).

los.text: Interpret an ultrasound scan (USS) report and swab results in the context of the patient's clinical presentation
los.html:
PID diagnostic interpretation
  • PID is a clinical diagnosis (lower abdominal pain + adnexal/cervical motion tenderness ± fever, discharge, IMB/PCB, dyspareunia)
  • Tests support but cannot exclude.
Swabs
  • NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea (endocervical/vulvovaginal) ± Mycoplasma genitalium
  • Gonorrhoea culture (sensitivities)
  • High vaginal swab (BV, trichomonas)
  • Positive result supports PID but negative doesn't exclude (many PID cases are polymicrobial/anaerobic).
  • Absence of pus cells on microscopy has good NPV.
USS report
  • Often normal in uncomplicated PID
  • May show thickened fluid-filled tubes (pyosalpinx/hydrosalpinx), free fluid, tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) (complex adnexal mass → admit, IV antibiotics ± drainage)
  • Also excludes alternatives (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst/torsion, appendicitis).
OtherPregnancy test (essential), CRP/WCC (raised supports), urinalysis/MSU, HIV and syphilis serology.
Integratee.g. "Lower abdominal pain, cervical excitation, positive chlamydia NAAT, USS shows small amount of free fluid and normal ovaries, hCG negative → PID; no abscess → outpatient treatment."

los.text: Explain the diagnosis of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) to the patient, including its causes, symptoms, and potential complications in language that all patients can understand
los.html:
Lay explanation"PID is an infection of the womb, the fallopian tubes and sometimes the ovaries. The fallopian tubes carry eggs from the ovaries to the womb."
Cause (lay)
  • "Bacteria travel up from the vagina or cervix.
  • Often this is a sexually transmitted infection like chlamydia or gonorrhoea, but other bacteria can do it too."
Symptoms
  • "It can cause pain low in the tummy, pain during sex, bleeding between periods or after sex, unusual discharge, and sometimes fever.
  • Some people have very mild symptoms."
Complications(explain sensitively, without alarming excessively)
  • "If it isn't treated quickly, it can scar the fallopian tubes, which can make it harder to get pregnant (infertility), increases the chance of a pregnancy developing outside the womb (ectopic pregnancy), and can cause long-term pelvic pain.
  • Rarely, a pocket of infection (abscess) can form.
  • Treating it early greatly lowers these risks."
Communication
  • Check what they already know
  • Use simple language and diagrams
  • Avoid blame/judgement
  • Check understanding (teach-back)
  • Address worries (fertility, partner, confidentiality)
  • Offer written information/leaflets.

los.text: Discuss the management of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), including medical and lifestyle interventions, with the patient
los.html:
Medical management (BASHH 2019, outpatient)
  • IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD + oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days (alternatives: ofloxacin + metronidazole 14 days; moxifloxacin if M. genitalium).
  • Start empirically (don't wait for results)
  • Analgesia
  • Review at 72 h (improvement expected; admit if not).
Admit for IV antibiotics if: severe illness/sepsis, TOA, pregnancy, surgical emergency not excluded, failure of oral treatment, unable to tolerate oral therapy.
IUD/IUSMay remain in situ if mild and responding (remove if no improvement after 72 h; consider emergency contraception if recent intercourse).
Partner notification and treatmentCurrent partner(s) and those in last 6 months tested and treated (doxycycline) even if asymptomatic → prevents reinfection.
Lifestyle/behavioural
  • Avoid sexual intercourse until both have completed treatment (and partner treated)
  • Condoms with new/casual partners
  • Full STI screen (HIV, syphilis)
  • Regular testing
  • Finish the full course
  • Return if worse/pregnancy symptoms
  • Smoking cessation (↑ risk)
  • Consider test of cure (gonorrhoea, M. genitalium, pregnancy).
Discuss fertility concerns and future pregnancy (early scan to exclude ectopic).

los.text: Identify and name commonly used equipment in obstetrics and gynaecology, recognising their purpose and appropriate context of use
los.html:
EquipmentPurpose
Cusco's (bivalve) speculumVisualise cervix/vagina: smears, swabs, IUD fitting
Sims' speculumAssess prolapse (vaginal walls), left lateral position
Cervical sampling brush (Cervex-Brush)Liquid-based cytology/HPV testing (cervical screening)
Swabs (charcoal/culture, NAAT, viral PCR)STIs, BV, candida, HSV
Pipelle endometrial samplerOutpatient endometrial biopsy
Hysteroscope (outpatient)View uterine cavity: polyps, fibroids, cancer, retained IUD
ColposcopeMagnified view of cervix with acetic acid/iodine (CIN), LLETZ
IUD/IUS insertion kit (tenaculum, uterine sound, insertion device)Contraception/HMB
Ring pessary/shelf pessaryConservative treatment of prolapse
Transvaginal ultrasound probeEarly pregnancy, ovaries, endometrial thickness
Pinard stethoscope / handheld Doppler (sonicaid)Fetal heart auscultation
CTG (cardiotocograph)Fetal heart rate + uterine contractions in labour/antenatal
AmnihookArtificial rupture of membranes (amniotomy)
Fetal scalp electrodeDirect fetal heart monitoring
Ventouse (Kiwi/vacuum cup) and obstetric forceps (Neville-Barnes, Kielland's for rotation)Assisted vaginal delivery
PartogramLabour progress chart
Tape measureSymphysis–fundal height
Bakri balloonTamponade for PPH
Urinary catheter, cord clamp, episiotomy scissors

los.text: Select and apply appropriate obstetric and gynaecological equipment in relevant clinical scenarios
los.html:
Scenario-based selection
  • Routine cervical screening → Cusco speculum + cytobrush, LBC pot.
  • Suspected STI/PID → Cusco speculum, NAAT swabs (endocervical/vulvovaginal), HVS.
  • Postmenopausal bleeding → TVUSS (endometrial thickness) → Pipelle biopsy/hysteroscopy.
  • Prolapse → Sims' speculum (left lateral), ring pessary fitting (measure, lubricate, insert).
  • HMB with no pathology → LNG-IUS insertion kit.
  • Abnormal smear → colposcopy ± LLETZ.
  • Antenatal check → tape measure (SFH), Doppler (fetal heart), BP, urine dipstick.
  • Labour: CTG (continuous if high risk), amnihook (ARM), fetal scalp electrode (poor contact/abnormal CTG), partogram.
  • Prolonged second stage/fetal distress with fully dilated cervix, head engaged → ventouse or forceps (forceps if preterm <34 weeks or face presentation; Kielland's for rotation).
  • PPH → bimanual uterine compression, uterotonics, Bakri balloon, catheter.
PrinciplesCorrect size, check function, aseptic technique, consent and chaperone, explain procedure.

los.text: Generate and justify a list of differential diagnoses for a range of obstetric and gynaecological presentations
los.html:
Obstetric presentations
  • Antepartum haemorrhage (>24 weeks): placental abruption (painful, tense "woody" uterus, may be concealed), placenta praevia (painless, high presenting part; no digital VE until USS), vasa praevia (fetal bleeding with ROM), cervical lesions, uterine rupture (previous CS).
  • Abdominal pain in pregnancy: labour (term/preterm), abruption, pre-eclampsia/HELLP (RUQ/epigastric), UTI/pyelonephritis, appendicitis, fibroid degeneration, ovarian torsion, constipation, round ligament pain, uterine rupture.
  • Hypertension/headache in pregnancy: pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, chronic HTN, migraine, CVST.
  • Breathlessness: physiological, anaemia, PE, peripartum cardiomyopathy, asthma.
  • Reduced fetal movements: fetal compromise/stillbirth, maternal factors → CTG, USS.
  • Itching: obstetric cholestasis (palms/soles, ↑ bile acids), eczema, PEP.
GynaecologicalSee ICM Year 2 › Reproductive & sexual health › LO 10 (pelvic pain, bleeding, discharge, masses, PMB).
Justify using features, gestation, risk factors (previous CS, smoking, cocaine, HTN) and investigations (USS, CTG, FBC, G&S, Kleihauer).
Placental abruptionPlacenta praevia
BleedingPainful; shock out of proportion to visible lossPainless bright red
UterusTender, tense ("woody")Soft; malpresentation common

los.text: Describe and apply the immediate management steps for patients presenting with ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), in line with national clinical guidelines
los.html:
Recognise STEMIIschaemic chest pain + ST elevation (or new LBBB/posterior MI) → activate primary PCI pathway.
Immediate management (NICE CG167/NG185, ESC)
  • ABCDE, cardiac monitoring, IV access, bloods (troponin, FBC, U&E, glucose, lipids, clotting), 12-lead ECG serial.
  • Aspirin 300 mg loading (chewed/dispersible).
  • Analgesia: IV morphine (titrated, e.g. 2.5–5 mg) + antiemetic (metoclopramide/cyclizine); GTN sublingual/IV if BP permits (avoid if SBP <90, RV infarct, PDE5i).
  • Oxygen only if SpO₂ <94% (target 94–98%; 88–92% if COPD).
  • Reperfusion: primary PCI if within 12 h of symptom onset and can be delivered within 120 min of when fibrinolysis could be given; otherwise fibrinolysis (tenecteplase) + antithrombin; then transfer for angiography.
  • Second antiplatelet (P2Y12 inhibitor) before/at PCI: prasugrel (if PCI, not on anticoagulant, age <75, no stroke history) or ticagrelor; clopidogrel if high bleeding risk or with anticoagulation.
  • Anticoagulation during PCI (unfractionated heparin; bivalirudin).
  • Treat complications: arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, heart failure.

los.text: Prescribe medications used in secondary prevention post-MI (e.g. statins, beta-blockers, antiplatelets) and explain their mechanisms of action
los.html:
DrugMechanismNotes
Aspirin 75 mg OD (lifelong)Irreversible COX-1 inhibition → ↓ thromboxane A₂ → ↓ platelet aggregationGI bleeding (PPI cover with DAPT)
P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 90 mg BD / prasugrel 10 mg OD / clopidogrel 75 mg OD) for 12 months (DAPT)Block ADP P2Y12 receptor on plateletsTicagrelor: dyspnoea, bleeding; prasugrel: avoid if prior stroke/TIA; clopidogrel prodrug (CYP2C19)
High-intensity statin: atorvastatin 80 mg ODHMG-CoA reductase inhibition → ↓ LDL, plaque stabilisationLFTs at baseline, 3 and 12 months; myalgia; target LDL ↓ (≤2.0 or ≤1.8 mmol/L)
β-blocker (bisoprolol, e.g. 2.5–10 mg OD)β1 blockade → ↓ HR, ↓ O₂ demand, anti-arrhythmic, ↓ remodellingEspecially if LVEF reduced; continue ≥12 months (long-term if HFrEF); caution asthma, bradycardia
ACE inhibitor (ramipril 2.5 mg → titrate to 10 mg)↓ Ang II → ↓ remodelling, afterloadStart early (days 1–3); check U&E/BP 1–2 weeks after each titration; ARB if intolerant
MRA (eplerenone)Aldosterone antagonismIf LVEF ≤40% with HF or diabetes (EPHESUS); check K⁺
SGLT2 inhibitorIf HFrEF/diabetes/CKD
PPI (lansoprazole/omeprazole: note omeprazole–clopidogrel interaction)GI protection with DAPT
GTN spray PRNNitrateSymptom relief
  • Plus: cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation, lifestyle, BP/diabetes control.

los.text: Identify and select appropriate antidepressant medications for patients post-cardiac event, considering drug safety and interactions
los.html:
Depression after MI/ACSCommon (~20%), ↑ mortality and non-adherence → screen (PHQ-2/9) and treat.
First choice: SSRIsSertraline (best evidence of safety post-MI: SADHART trial; minimal QT effect, few CYP interactions) (citalopram/escitalopram: dose-dependent QT prolongation: max citalopram 20 mg in >65 or cardiac disease).
AvoidTricyclic antidepressants (arrhythmias, QT, postural hypotension, anticholinergic tachycardia, lethal in overdose), venlafaxine (↑ BP, HR), MAOIs.
MirtazapineAlternative (weight gain, sedation; some evidence: MIND-IT).
Interactions to consider
  • SSRIs + antiplatelets/anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk (give PPI gastroprotection, especially with DAPT)
  • Hyponatraemia (with diuretics)
  • Fluoxetine/paroxetine CYP2D6 inhibition (↑ β-blockers like metoprolol)
  • Clopidogrel–fluoxetine/fluvoxamine (CYP2C19)
  • Serotonin syndrome with tramadol.
Non-drugCBT, cardiac rehabilitation (psychological support), social support, exercise.

los.text: Complete a safe and accurate discharge prescription for post-MI patients and communicate relevant follow-up plans and medication changes to primary care
los.html:
Discharge prescription (TTO) essentials
  • Patient details
  • Allergies
  • Diagnosis ("anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI to LAD with drug-eluting stent on [date]")
  • All medicines with generic name
  • Dose
  • Route
  • Frequency
  • Duration (e.g. "ticagrelor 90 mg BD for 12 months: stop [date]")
  • Indication
  • and status (new/changed/stopped, with reasons)
  • PRN medications (GTN)
  • Legible
  • Signed and dated
  • Check for interactions and duplications
  • Renal dosing.
Typical post-MI discharge medications
  • Aspirin 75 mg lifelong
  • Ticagrelor/prasugrel/clopidogrel for 12 months
  • Atorvastatin 80 mg
  • Bisoprolol
  • Ramipril (titrating)
  • ± eplerenone, SGLT2i
  • PPI
  • GTN spray
  • ± antidepressant
  • Stopped drugs (e.g. NSAIDs) documented.
Communication to primary care (discharge letter)
  • Diagnosis, procedures, complications, LVEF (echo).
  • Medication changes and rationale, DAPT stop date, titration plans (ACEi/β-blocker up-titration targets), monitoring required (U&E in 1–2 weeks, lipids/LFTs at 3 months, BP, HR).
  • Follow-up: cardiology clinic, cardiac rehabilitation referral, HF nurse if LVEF reduced, echo repeat.
  • Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet, exercise, alcohol; driving (DVLA: car 1 week after successful PCI with LVEF >40% and no further revascularisation planned; otherwise 4 weeks; Group 2 longer), return to work, sexual activity (~4 weeks; avoid PDE5i with nitrates).
  • Safety-netting: what to do if chest pain recurs (GTN, call 999).
Patient counsellingPurpose of each drug, side effects, importance of not stopping antiplatelets (stent thrombosis), carry GTN.

los.text: Perform a structured neck and thyroid status examination and identify clinical signs associated with thyroid dysfunction or pathology
los.html:
Neck examination
  • Inspection (front, sides): goitre, scars (thyroidectomy), swelling, skin changes; ask patient to swallow water (thyroid and thyroglossal cysts rise) and protrude tongue (thyroglossal cyst rises; thyroid doesn't).
  • Palpation from behind: thyroid (isthmus below cricoid, lobes): size, shape (diffuse/multinodular/solitary nodule), consistency, tenderness, mobility, swallow while palpating; lymph nodes (cervical chains); trachea position; can you get below the goitre (retrosternal extension: percuss sternum).
  • Auscultation: thyroid bruit (Graves': ↑ vascularity).
  • Pemberton's sign: arms raised above head → facial plethora/congestion (retrosternal goitre, thoracic inlet obstruction).
Thyroid status
  • Hands: sweaty/warm (hyper) or cool/dry (hypo), fine tremor (outstretched hands with paper), palmar erythema, thyroid acropachy (clubbing-like: Graves'), onycholysis.
  • Pulse: tachycardia/AF (hyper) or bradycardia (hypo); BP.
  • Eyes (Graves' ophthalmopathy): lid retraction, lid lag (follow finger down), exophthalmos/proptosis (from side and above), chemosis, ophthalmoplegia (eye movements, diplopia), visual acuity (optic neuropathy).
  • Legs: pretibial myxoedema (Graves'), oedema; slow-relaxing ankle reflexes (hypothyroid); proximal myopathy (stand from squat/chair: hyperthyroid).
  • General: weight, agitation vs slowness, hair/skin changes, voice (hoarse in hypothyroid).

los.text: Present clinical findings from the neck/thyroid status examination clearly, using structured and concise medical terminology
los.html:
Template
  • "On examination, Ms X appeared [anxious/restless/slow], with [no] obvious goitre on inspection.
  • Palpation revealed a [diffusely enlarged, smooth, non-tender] goitre that moved with swallowing but not with tongue protrusion; [no] retrosternal extension; a [thyroid bruit] was audible.
  • There was [no] cervical lymphadenopathy; trachea central."
Thyroid status
  • "Clinically [hyperthyroid/euthyroid/hypothyroid]", then list the evidence:
  • Hands: warm sweaty palms, fine tremor. Pulse: 110 bpm, irregularly irregular.
  • Eyes: lid retraction, lid lag, bilateral exophthalmos, no ophthalmoplegia.
  • Other: pretibial myxoedema, brisk reflexes, proximal weakness.
Summary
  • "These findings are consistent with Graves' disease with thyroid eye disease and atrial fibrillation.
  • I would request TFTs, TSH receptor antibodies, thyroid USS ± uptake scan, ECG, and refer to endocrinology and ophthalmology."
For a noduleDescribe site (left/right lobe, isthmus), size, consistency (hard: malignancy concern), mobility, nodes, voice (hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve) → USS ± FNA.

los.text: Identify features of the bony pelvis and define the terms 'greater' and 'lesser' pelvis.
los.html:
Bony pelvisTwo hip (innominate) bones (each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis at the acetabulum, fused by ~16–18 yrs), sacrum and coccyx.
Features
  • Ilium (iliac crest, ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, PIIS, iliac fossa, auricular surface, greater sciatic notch)
  • Ischium (ischial spine, ischial tuberosity, lesser sciatic notch, ramus)
  • Pubis (body, superior and inferior rami, pubic tubercle, pubic crest, pubic symphysis, pecten pubis)
  • Obturator foramen (closed by obturator membrane)
  • Acetabulum
  • Pelvic brim (linea terminalis)
  • Sacral promontory.
Greater (false) pelvisAbove the pelvic brim, between iliac fossae; part of abdominal cavity (supports abdominal viscera: ileum, sigmoid colon).
Lesser (true) pelvis
  • Below the pelvic brim: contains pelvic viscera (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs)
  • Bounded by the pelvic inlet above and pelvic outlet (closed by pelvic floor) below
  • Forms the birth canal.

los.text: Demonstrate the main palpable anatomical landmarks of the iliac, ischial and pubic bones in the living, on bones and suitable radiographs
los.html:
Palpable landmarks in the living
  • Iliac crest (top at L4 level: Tuffier's line for lumbar puncture), ASIS (anterior end of crest; inguinal ligament attachment), iliac tubercle (~5 cm behind ASIS), PSIS (posterior; dimples of Venus at S2 level: sacroiliac joint).
  • Pubic tubercle (lateral to symphysis; inguinal ligament attaches; landmark for hernias), pubic crest, pubic symphysis.
  • Ischial tuberosity (sitting bone; palpable in buttock with hip flexed), ischial spine (on vaginal/rectal exam: pudendal block landmark), coccyx (natal cleft), sacrum.
  • Greater trochanter (femur; lateral hip).
On bonesIdentify all parts of ilium/ischium/pubis (LO 31), acetabulum, obturator foramen, sciatic notches/foramina (with sacrospinous/sacrotuberous ligaments).
On radiographs (AP pelvis)
  • Iliac wings
  • Sacrum and sacral foramina
  • Sacroiliac joints
  • Pubic symphysis
  • Obturator foramina (symmetry: rotation)
  • Acetabula and femoral heads
  • Iliopectineal and ilioischial lines (anterior and posterior columns: acetabular fractures)
  • Shenton's line
  • Ischial tuberosities
  • Greater/lesser trochanters
  • Pelvic ring (fractures usually in ≥2 places).

los.text: Identify and describe the joints and ligaments of the pelvis.
los.html:
JointTypeLigaments
Sacroiliac jointsSynovial (plane) anteriorly + fibrous (syndesmosis) posteriorly; very limited movement (nutation; ↑ in pregnancy)
  • Anterior sacroiliac, interosseous sacroiliac (strongest), posterior sacroiliac ligaments
  • Accessory: sacrotuberous (sacrum → ischial tuberosity) and sacrospinous (sacrum → ischial spine) ligaments (resist sacral tilting; convert sciatic notches into greater and lesser sciatic foramina)
  • Iliolumbar ligament (L5 transverse process → iliac crest)
Pubic symphysisSecondary cartilaginous (fibrocartilaginous disc between hyaline-covered bones)Superior pubic and inferior (arcuate) pubic ligaments
Lumbosacral jointIV disc + facet jointsIliolumbar ligaments
Sacrococcygeal jointCartilaginousSacrococcygeal ligaments
Hip jointSynovial ball-and-socketIliofemoral (Y-ligament: strongest), pubofemoral, ischiofemoral, ligamentum teres, labrum
Pregnancy
  • Relaxin/progesterone → ligament laxity → widening of symphysis and SIJ mobility → ↑ pelvic diameter for birth
  • Symphysis pubis dysfunction/pelvic girdle pain.
ClinicalSacroiliitis (ankylosing spondylitis), pelvic ring fractures (unstable if both anterior and posterior ring disrupted: open-book).

los.text: Identify the boundaries and major features of the pelvic inlet and the component parts of the pelvic outlet (recognising their normal orientation).
los.html:
Pelvic inlet (superior aperture)
  • Bounded by the sacral promontory and alae (posteriorly)
  • Arcuate line of ilium
  • Pectineal line (pecten pubis)
  • Pubic crest and upper border of pubic symphysis (anteriorly) = pelvic brim/linea terminalis.
  • In the female typically round/oval (gynaecoid)
  • Widest transverse diameter.
  • Orientation: plane tilted ~50–60° to the horizontal in standing (ASIS and pubic tubercle in same vertical plane).
Pelvic outlet (inferior aperture)
  • Diamond-shaped
  • Bounded by pubic symphysis (inferior margin) and pubic arch (ischiopubic rami) anteriorly
  • Ischial tuberosities laterally
  • Sacrotuberous ligaments posterolaterally
  • and tip of coccyx posteriorly
  • Widest anteroposterior diameter (coccyx moves back in labour).
  • Closed by the pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) and perineum.
Diameters (obstetric relevance)
  • Inlet: AP (obstetric) conjugate (sacral promontory → posterior symphysis, ~11 cm), transverse (~13 cm), oblique
  • Mid-pelvis: interspinous diameter (~10 cm: narrowest; ischial spines = station 0)
  • Outlet: AP (~12.5 cm), transverse (intertuberous, ~11 cm).
Fetal head enters inlet occipito-transverse (widest transverse), rotates at mid-pelvis to occipito-anterior to exit through the outlet's widest AP diameter.

los.text: Compare and contrast the female and male pelvis.
los.html:
FeatureFemale (gynaecoid)Male (android)
General structureThinner, lighter, smootherThicker, heavier, more prominent muscle markings
Pelvic inletOval/round, wider transverselyHeart-shaped
Pelvic outletWider (everted ischial tuberosities)Narrower
Pelvic cavityWide, shallow, cylindricalNarrow, deep, funnel-shaped
Subpubic angle (pubic arch)Wide (>80–90°), U-shapedNarrow (~50–60°), V-shaped
Greater sciatic notchWide (~90°)Narrow (~70°)
Ischial spinesLess prominent (wider interspinous diameter)Prominent, inturned
Obturator foramenOval/triangularRound
AcetabulumSmaller, faces anterolaterallyLarger, faces laterally
SacrumShorter, wider, less curvedLonger, narrower, more curved
Iliac wingsFlaredMore vertical
ReasonFemale pelvis adapted for childbirth (wider inlet/outlet/cavity).
Other shapes(Caldwell–Moloy)Anthropoid (oval AP: favours OP), platypelloid (flat), android in females (risk of obstructed labour/deep transverse arrest).

los.text: Describe and identify the boundaries, divisions and structures within the perineum.
los.html:
PerineumDiamond-shaped region below the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani), between the thighs.
Boundaries
  • Anterior: pubic symphysis (inferior margin)
  • Anterolateral: ischiopubic rami
  • Lateral: ischial tuberosities
  • Posterolateral: sacrotuberous ligaments
  • Posterior: coccyx
  • Roof: pelvic floor (levator ani)
  • Floor: skin and fascia.
Divisions(by a line between the ischial tuberosities)Anterior urogenital triangle and posterior anal triangle.
Urogenital triangle
  • Perineal membrane (thick fascial sheet spanning the pubic arch) divides it into: deep perineal pouch (above membrane: external urethral sphincter, compressor urethrae, deep transverse perineal muscles, bulbourethral glands (male), part of urethra) and superficial perineal pouch (below membrane: erectile tissue (crura/clitoris or penis, bulbs), ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal muscles, greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands (female), perineal vessels and nerves)
  • External genitalia
  • Urethra and vagina pass through.
Anal triangleAnal canal, external anal sphincter, ischioanal fossae (fat, pudendal canal with internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve), anococcygeal body.
Perineal body at centre between the triangles.

los.text: Describe and identify the components of the anterior and posterior pelvic wall and pelvic floor.
los.html:
Anterior pelvic wallBodies of pubic bones, pubic symphysis, superior pubic rami (bladder lies behind).
Lateral pelvic walls
  • Hip bones (ilium/ischium/pubis below brim) with obturator foramen covered by obturator membrane and obturator internus muscle (leaves via lesser sciatic foramen to insert on greater trochanter)
  • Obturator fascia gives origin to levator ani (tendinous arch)
  • Obturator nerve and vessels run along it.
Posterior pelvic wallSacrum and coccyx, piriformis (from anterior sacrum → through greater sciatic foramen → greater trochanter), sacral plexus on piriformis, sacroiliac joints, coccygeus.
Pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm)
  • Funnel/hammock of levator ani (pubococcygeus incl. puborectalis and pubovaginalis/levator prostatae, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus (ischiococcygeus), with superior and inferior fascia
  • Gap anteriorly (urogenital hiatus: urethra, vagina) and opening for anal canal.
FunctionsSupport pelvic viscera, resist ↑ intra-abdominal pressure, maintain urinary and faecal continence, role in childbirth (guides fetal head rotation), sexual function.

los.text: Demonstrate the points of attachment of the muscles of the abdominal wall and those of the levator ani.
los.html:
Abdominal wall muscle attachments to pelvis
  • Rectus abdominis: pubic crest and pubic symphysis → xiphoid and costal cartilages 5–7.
  • External oblique: ribs 5–12 → iliac crest (anterior half), pubic tubercle, linea alba; lower free border forms the inguinal ligament (ASIS → pubic tubercle); superficial ring.
  • Internal oblique: thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lateral ⅔ of inguinal ligament → lower ribs, linea alba, pubic crest/pecten via conjoint tendon.
  • Transversus abdominis: lower costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lateral ⅓ inguinal ligament → linea alba, pubic crest and pecten (conjoint tendon).
  • Pyramidalis: pubic body → linea alba.
  • Quadratus lumborum: iliolumbar ligament, iliac crest → 12th rib, lumbar transverse processes.
Levator ani attachments
  • Origin: posterior surface of body of pubis, tendinous arch of the obturator internus fascia, ischial spine.
  • Insertion: perineal body, walls of vagina/prostate, rectum and anal canal (puborectalis sling behind anorectal junction), anococcygeal ligament (raphe), coccyx.
  • Demonstrate on skeleton/model: pubic crest, pubic tubercle, ASIS, iliac crest, inguinal ligament line
  • Inner pubis, obturator fascia arch to ischial spine.

los.text: Discuss the functions of the pelvic floor musculature, its midline raphe and the structures passing through it in females.
los.html:
Functions of pelvic floor musculature
  • Support of pelvic organs (bladder, uterus, vagina, rectum) against gravity and ↑ intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, lifting) → prevents prolapse.
  • Continence: urinary (compression of urethra against anterior vaginal wall support; external urethral sphincter) and faecal (puborectalis anorectal angle, external anal sphincter).
  • Childbirth: the funnel shape and gutter of levator ani guide the fetal head to rotate (to OA) and descend; stretches massively (→ injury: levator avulsion, pudendal nerve stretch).
  • Sexual function (contributes to vaginal tone, orgasm).
  • Respiration/posture: part of the core muscle "canister" with diaphragm and abdominal muscles.
Midline raphe
  • Anococcygeal raphe/body (between anus and coccyx), where the iliococcygeus fibres of each side interdigitate
  • Provides attachment and a firm posterior support (levator plate) on which pelvic organs rest.
Structures passing through the pelvic floor (female)
  • Urethra, vagina (through the urogenital hiatus anteriorly), anal canal/rectum (posteriorly)
  • Plus nerves/vessels at the periphery (pudendal vessels/nerve via greater/lesser sciatic foramina, not through levator).
ClinicalObstetric trauma → stress incontinence, prolapse (cystocele, rectocele, uterine), faecal incontinence; pelvic floor muscle training.

los.text: Describe and identify the location of the perineal membrane and the perineal body.
los.html:
Perineal membrane
  • Thick triangular fascial sheet stretching between the ischiopubic rami across the anterior (urogenital) triangle
  • Separates the deep perineal pouch (above) from the superficial perineal pouch (below)
  • Pierced by the urethra (and vagina in females)
  • Gives attachment to the erectile tissue (bulbs, crura) and perineal muscles
  • Posterior free border attached to the perineal body.
Perineal body (central tendon of the perineum)
  • Irregular fibromuscular mass at the centre of the perineum, between the vagina (or bulb of penis) and anal canal, at the junction of urogenital and anal triangles.
  • Muscles attaching: bulbospongiosus, superficial and deep transverse perineal, external anal sphincter, levator ani (pubovaginalis/puboperinealis), external urethral sphincter fibres, longitudinal rectal muscle.
FunctionAnchors pelvic floor and perineal muscles; critical for pelvic floor integrity and support of posterior vaginal wall.
Clinical
  • Perineal tears in childbirth (1st: skin; 2nd: perineal muscles/perineal body; 3rd: anal sphincter; 4th: + anal mucosa) and episiotomy (mediolateral, to avoid extending into sphincter)
  • → poor repair
  • → prolapse (rectocele), faecal incontinence, dyspareunia.

los.text: Describe the origins, courses and relations of the uterine and ovarian arteries.
los.html:
Uterine artery
  • Branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery
  • → runs medially in the base of the broad ligament (cardinal ligament)
  • → crosses superior (anterior) to the ureter ~1.5–2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge": ureter is the water, artery the bridge)
  • → reaches the uterus at the level of the internal os
  • → ascends tortuously along the lateral uterine wall within the broad ligament
  • → anastomoses with the ovarian artery near the uterine tube
  • Gives vaginal (cervicovaginal) branches downwards
  • Supplies uterus, cervix, upper vagina, medial uterine tube.
  • In pregnancy enlarges massively (~500–750 mL/min to placenta).
Ovarian artery
  • Arises from the abdominal aorta (~L2, below renal arteries)
  • → descends retroperitoneally on psoas, crosses the ureter (anteriorly) and external iliac vessels at pelvic brim
  • → enters the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament of the ovary
  • → mesovarium to the ovary
  • Branches to uterine tube
  • Anastomoses with uterine artery in the broad ligament.
Venous
  • Ovarian veins → right to IVC, left to left renal vein (left varicocele/pelvic congestion analogy)
  • Uterine veins → internal iliac veins.
Clinical
  • Hysterectomy: clamping the uterine artery risks ureteric injury (close relationship lateral to cervix)
  • Infundibulopelvic ligament contains ovarian vessels (ligated in oophorectomy; ureter nearby at pelvic brim)
  • Uterine artery embolisation for fibroids/PPH
  • Ovarian torsion twists the ovarian vessels.

los.text: Describe the paths and innervations of the pudendal nerves, and the sites that may be injected for anaesthesia during childbirth.
los.html:
Pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4)
  • From the sacral plexus
  • → leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis)
  • → crosses the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament (medial to internal pudendal vessels)
  • → re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the perineum
  • → runs in the pudendal (Alcock's) canal (on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa, in obturator fascia) with internal pudendal vessels.
Branches
  • Inferior rectal (anal) nerve: external anal sphincter, perianal skin, anal canal below pectinate line.
  • Perineal nerve: superficial branch (labial/scrotal skin) and deep branch (superficial and deep perineal muscles: bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, transverse perineal, external urethral sphincter).
  • Dorsal nerve of clitoris (or penis): sensory to clitoris/penis.
Function("S2, 3, 4 keeps the penis off the floor" and continence)Sensation of perineum/external genitalia, voluntary control of urethral and anal sphincters, orgasm/ejaculation.
Pudendal nerve block (childbirth)
  • Local anaesthetic injected transvaginally around the ischial spine (palpated through the lateral vaginal wall)
  • Just medial and posterior to the spine through the sacrospinous ligament → anaesthesia of perineum for instrumental delivery
  • Episiotomy repair
  • Perineal suturing
  • Avoid internal pudendal vessels (aspirate).
  • Also perineal infiltration for episiotomy
  • Epidural/spinal for labour analgesia/caesarean (lumbar).
ClinicalStretching/compression in prolonged labour → pudendal neuropathy → faecal/urinary incontinence; pudendal neuralgia (cyclists).

los.text: Explain the function of the greater vestibular glands (Bartholin's glands )
los.html:
Greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands
  • Pea-sized glands in the superficial perineal pouch, posterolateral to the vaginal orifice, deep to the posterior ends of the bulbs of the vestibule (and covered by bulbospongiosus)
  • Homologous to male bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.
Ducts open into the vestibule on each side of the vaginal orifice at ~4 and 8 o'clock (between hymen and labia minora).
FunctionSecrete mucus during sexual arousal → lubrication of the vestibule and vaginal introitus; also keep vulval mucosa moist. Parasympathetic stimulation.
Clinical
  • Duct obstruction → Bartholin's cyst (painless swelling of posterior labium majus)
  • Infection
  • → Bartholin's abscess (painful, tender, red swelling; polymicrobial, sometimes gonococcal/chlamydial)
  • → incision and drainage with Word catheter or marsupialisation, antibiotics if cellulitis
  • Carcinoma rare (biopsy if >40 and new mass).

los.text: Identify the recto-uterine (pouch of Douglas) and the vesico-uterine pouch.
los.html:
• Peritoneal pouches in the female pelvis (peritoneum draping over pelvic organs):
  • Vesico-uterine pouch: shallow recess between the bladder (anteriorly) and uterus (body) (posteriorly); usually empty; incised at caesarean section (lower segment approach: bladder reflected down).
  • Recto-uterine pouch (pouch of Douglas): deeper recess between the uterus/posterior fornix of vagina (anteriorly) and rectum (posteriorly); lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the upright/supine female → fluid, blood, pus collect here.
Clinical significance of pouch of Douglas
  • Free fluid/blood (ruptured ectopic, ruptured cyst) seen on TVUSS; historically culdocentesis via posterior fornix.
  • Pelvic abscess (appendicitis, PID, post-op) → palpable/tender on PV/PR examination; drainage via posterior fornix/rectum.
  • Endometriosis deposits (nodules, obliteration of pouch, deep dyspareunia), metastatic deposits (ovarian/gastric cancer: Blumer's shelf), ascites.
  • Access for posterior colpotomy and laparoscopic visualisation.
Male equivalentRectovesical pouch (between bladder and rectum).

los.text: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the pelvis.
los.html:
• Principle: pelvic lymph follows blood vessels → internal iliac, external iliac, common iliac, sacral and para-aortic nodes
    • external structures/skin → superficial inguinal nodes.
OrganLymph drainage
OvariesPara-aortic (lumbar) nodes (along ovarian vessels, at L1–L2)
Uterine fundus/upper bodyPara-aortic nodes (with ovarian vessels); some to superficial inguinal via round ligament
Uterine body/lower segmentExternal iliac nodes
CervixExternal iliac, internal iliac (obturator), sacral nodes → common iliac → para-aortic (cervical cancer staging: pelvic lymphadenectomy)
Upper vaginaInternal and external iliac
Lower vagina (below hymen), vulva, clitoris, perineal skinSuperficial inguinal nodes (vulval cancer: bilateral spread near midline)
BladderExternal and internal iliac
RectumPararectal → inferior mesenteric (upper), internal iliac (middle/lower); anal canal below pectinate line → superficial inguinal
ProstateInternal iliac, obturator, sacral
TestesPara-aortic (not inguinal)
  • Clinical: cancer staging and spread (ovarian cancer → para-aortic nodes + transcoelomic spread; cervical → pelvic nodes; vulval → inguinal), surgical lymphadenectomy → lower limb lymphoedema.

los.text: Interpret standard diagnostic images of the pelvis and be able to recognise common abnormalities
los.html:
Imaging modalities
  • AP pelvis X-ray (bones, joints, fractures, calcifications, IUD)
  • Pelvic ultrasound (transabdominal (full bladder) and transvaginal: uterus, endometrium, ovaries, pregnancy, free fluid)
  • CT (trauma, abscess, staging)
  • MRI (gynae-oncology staging, fibroids/adenomyosis, endometriosis, rectal cancer, prostate)
  • Hysterosalpingography (tubal patency)
  • DEXA.
Common abnormalities
  • X-ray: pelvic fractures (pubic rami (elderly falls), acetabular, pelvic ring/open book (symphysis diastasis >2.5 cm), sacral insufficiency), OA hip, sacroiliitis (ankylosing spondylitis: erosions, sclerosis, fusion), Paget's disease (thickened trabeculae, enlarged bone), metastases (lytic: breast, renal; sclerotic: prostate), calcifications (phleboliths, fibroids (popcorn), bladder stones, vascular), IUD, dermoid (teeth), DDH.
  • USS: fibroids, ovarian cysts (simple vs complex), endometrial thickening (PMB: >4 mm abnormal), ectopic pregnancy (adnexal mass, empty uterus, free fluid), intrauterine pregnancy/miscarriage, PCOS morphology (≥20 follicles/ovary), hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, bladder volume.
  • MRI/CT: adenomyosis, deep endometriosis, cancer staging (cervix, endometrium, ovary), collections.
ApproachSystematic review (bones (rings: pelvic ring, obturator foramina), joints, soft tissues), compare sides, correlate clinically.
